title: Understanding the Accelerated Dragon!! | Open Sicilian | GM Naroditsky's Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We have Black against a strong player and answer the king's-pawn with c5 — the Sicilian.
White develops the knight to f3.
The knight to c6, heading for a mainline Accelerated Dragon.
White strikes with the pawn to d4 — the Open Sicilian.
We capture on d4.
White recaptures with the knight — music to my ears.
The pawn to g6, the Accelerated Dragon fianchetto — only our second of the whole run.
White plays the knight to c3 — the other main line, as opposed to the Maroczy Bind with c4.
Against the Maroczy Bind with c4, I have a sideline where you play the knight to f6 before fianchettoing.
But the knight to c3 is the other main line.
The bishop to g7, developing and pressuring the d4-knight down the long diagonal.
White develops the bishop to e3 — the main line.
Newer players tend to capture on c6 here, which is an immediate concession: Black recaptures toward the centre and the open b-file lets the rook pressure b2.
So the bishop to e3 is a no-brainer at higher levels. A mainline Dragon player would play d6 here — but from an Accelerated standpoint that lets White transition to a mainline Dragon with f3.
So we keep it uniquely Accelerated by developing the knight to f6 first — not pushing any central pawns yet, maybe not for several more moves.

White plays the queen to d2 — a not-especially-good sideline; the main is the bishop to c4. In any Dragon setup, once the queen leaves d1, consider the knight to g4: trading it for White's dark-squared bishop leaves our Dragon bishop uncontested. After the knight to g4 the bishop can't move — it would drop the twice-attacked d4-knight — though White can take on c6 and shift the bishop to d4.
We castle. And we don't play d6, which would let White transition to the Dragon with f3 — keeping the pawn on d7 means we can later strike with d5 in one move.

White castles queenside. Now the king and queen are aligned, so we recalculate the knight to g4: if White takes c6 and plays the bishop to d4, we have the bishop to h6, pinning the queen. White blocks with f4 — but then the pawn to e5 is winning.
The knight to g4 — hitting the f4-pawn, threatening the capture on f4, and attacking the d4-bishop: a simple double attack that costs White at least a piece.
White takes on c6.

We recapture with the b-pawn, ruining White's structure and opening the b-file — with White castled queenside that often spells immediate doom. The queen to b6 hits f2, which the g4-knight also attacks; the pawn to e5 chasing the bishop is another plan.
White plays the bishop to d4.
We respond instantly with the bishop to h6, pinning the queen.
White plays the pawn to f4, walking right into the losing line.

The pawn to e5 — the crusher. With the queen pinned, the f4-pawn can't move, so it's as if it isn't there and e5 wins. White's best is to take on e5 and decline the recapture, down a full piece. Then the attack is decisive: the c3-pawn becomes a battering ram shattering White's queenside cover, the queen to b6 threatens mate in one plus a check on e3, and the lobster-pincer mate with the queen reaching a3 finishes it — first opening the centre with d5 so the king finds no relief, and connecting the rooks with the bishop to g4 to bring a rook to d8.

An easy game — the Accelerated is the Sicilian nobody studies, and when you're on your own in a Sicilian, bad things happen. Against the Maroczy the recommendation is the knight to f6 first, setting a trap: if White grabs and pushes e5, there's a fork on the king and pawn. And in an earlier game White's bishop to e3 was a positional mistake punished by the knight to g4 — trading the knight for the bishop for uncontested dark squares.
With precise play White is slightly better, but it's a very playable position that's easy to learn.
We're facing the knight to c3 and the bishop to e3.
The bishop to g7 and the bishop to e3.
After the knight to f6, the queen to d2.
The queen to d2 is a move I honestly hadn't come across.
And the engine confirms castling is the correct reply — so we made the right decision.
Why avoid the mainline Dragon? It and the Accelerated are completely different animals.
The mainline Dragon and the Accelerated produce utterly different positions.
The traditional Dragon runs through the pawn to d6 and d4.
That's the entry point to the Najdorf and the Dragon.
The Najdorf with a6, which I could also have recommended.
The Dragon with g6 isn't refuted, but it's ridiculously risky and demands loads of theory.
The bishop to e3 — and even knowing tons of theory you can still get mated; the Dragon's standing is a bit dubious.
So players are more likely to study the Dragon from White's side than the Accelerated.
The key distinction: in the mainline Dragon White plays f3, and the main line runs the knight to c6 and the queen to d2.
The knight to c6.
The queen to d2 and castling, normally into opposite-side castling.
That's one main line.
In the other, White develops first.
The bishop to c4 to stop d5 — the Yugoslav Attack.
In the line where Black plays d5.
Castling and the pawn to d5.
The capture on d5 and the recapture with the knight.
The knight takes c6 and the recapture — the most popular line nowadays.
White plays the bishop to d4 — that same idea of taking Black's fianchetto bishop out of commission.
And Black is often forced into the undesirable pawn to e5.
The bishop to c5, closing the diagonal — which takes a lot of the fun out of the Dragon; a very popular line where White is considered better.
The rook to e8 — Black often sacrifices the exchange here, though Giri recommends this relatively rare rook move.

Back to the Accelerated — the important point, a trap even Fischer fell into: White tries the same idea with f3 and the queen to d2, but since we haven't committed to d6, we save a tempo and strike with d5 in one move. The same position arises in the mainline Dragon but with White to move; here it's White who must react, and after the capture on d5 we have a simple discovery, the knight to c4, leaving Black much better — the queen to a5 gives a great position against White's damaged structure.
